items.answer: I think the focus of the research team is more focused nowadays on the post-training, getting more performance out of that, because it's more like the newer paradigm and there are still low-hanging fruits to be picked. items.question: Why do you see tool use as an important direction for improving LLM answers?
items.object: LLM tool use
items.answer: I think there's a more heavy focus on tool use. Back then, when ChatGPT was launched or also the first iteration of LLMs, the focus was mainly on general-purpose tasks, but then also having the LLM answer all the things we are curious about from memory. If we ask it a math question or a knowledge question, the LLM would basically draw from its memory and then write the answer, but that's not always the most effective or accurate thing to do. Similar for us humans. I mean, LLMs are different from how humans think, but if you asked me a complicated math question, like multiplying two large numbers, I would pull out my calculator. I wouldn't do that in my head. I maybe could, but it would take a long time. It's more error-prone and so forth, and there's no need to do that. The same with LLMs. Now with more modern tooling it becomes more and more popular to use, or to have the LLM use, tools too. It requires training the LLM to use those tools, but with that I think we can reduce hallucination rates, not completely getting rid of those but reducing those, and also making answers more accurate.

items.question: How do you distinguish the contribution of LLM tooling from improvements in the models themselves to the practical quality of today's AI assistants?
items.object: LLM tooling, open-weight models, and harness engineering
items.answer: On the open-weight front, I think that's a separate thing where you have now companies developing the tooling around LLMs that is becoming more and more mature, and then you have better LLMs themselves. I think I would almost separate those two. My hypothesis is if you would take the best open-weight LLM and put it into, let's say, a ChatGPT or Gemini or Claude interface, you would almost get the same type of quality, performance, and everything. items.question: How do you like an LLM assistant to fit into your coding workflow?
items.object: LLM assistants integrated into a coding workflow
items.answer: I use Visual Studio Code, the code editor, for years, maybe five years now, ten years, and before that I was using Vim and other things, but I'm very familiar with the UI. I have my git tree. I know where I have a terminal inside. I actually liked having the LLM as a plugin there where you sometimes can say, "Okay, I have a bug. Can you just double-check?" It's just another layer of tools you add to your workflow. The LLM doesn't have to be front and center. It can be this little helper. I still debug things myself, but often it's quite nice and fast to ask the LLM to double-check things. What I like about it is when it's like a second pair of eyes, but it's also not completely taking over and doing everything. You as the person still have to ask the right questions and run the experiments to see whether it actually makes the code faster. items.answer: We still have the distinction between the different reasoning efforts, in terms of how much time the LLM should spend on getting you the results. items.question: How do you find LLMs useful for building tools for your everyday workflows?
items.object: Using LLMs to develop personal productivity apps
items.answer:
For my workflows, I don't have anything super automated where I need to run something incrementally or in an agentic type of setting. What I've been doing a lot, though, is developing my own apps, productivity apps. I grew up as a coder using bash, the terminal and Python, where I was writing myself scripts for all kinds of things to automate things. Now with LLMs I kind of changed that a bit towards developing native Mac OS apps. I always wanted to learn Swift coding. I've never had the time because there are so many other more important things to do for me. That was an opportunity to say, "I want this, what I have as a script, as a native Mac OS app," because it's just more convenient.

For example, just the other day my wife, who also has a podcast, a book club podcast, and I help her with the episodes, uploading everything and editing and the workflow in general because she's not a tech person. I had a script to add chapter marks to the podcast. The other day I made a native Mac OS app where you can just add the timestamps and click a button and it adds the chapter marks to the audio file. Simple things like that, and then I can share it with her and she can use it now. It's these little quality-of-life things in your everyday life where instead of doing things manually you can automate them now. This is not running the LLM, but it's using the LLM to develop something that behaves deterministically.

items.question: How do you decide when to use an LLM to perform a task versus to develop a deterministic tool for it?
items.object: Using LLMs to develop deterministic tools
items.answer: I think that's an important point: in these cases the LLM is not doing the regular work, the task. It's more developing the tool to do the task. The LLM is very useful and very capable, but there are tasks where it's almost wasteful to use an LLM for that. It's like if all you have is a hammer, everything becomes a nail, type of situation. If you have a deterministic task, it still makes sense to develop a deterministic tool. You can use an LLM for that, but it is almost wasteful to ask an LLM, "What is one plus one?" You can use a calculator. It's important to recognize what is the nature of this problem and what is the best tool for that problem.

items.question: Why do you think learning math and coding is still worthwhile when LLMs can do those things?
items.object: The value of learning math and coding when LLMs can perform those tasks
items.answer: I think it is actually still worthwhile to learn math and coding even though there are LLMs that can do that, because it makes your life more efficient and makes you better at using these LLMs. An example: I was using an LLM for my website to add a dark mode. I wrote the website myself like 12 years ago, but I knew HTML and CSS and JavaScript much better back then than I do now. I always procrastinated on adding a dark mode button because I knew it would take me like a month to do it well, and it's not my main job. But then I tried using an LLM for that, and it did a really good job adding it, but it was not perfect. The button was misaligned. I said, "Make it a bit higher, make it a bit lower, move it to the left," and I thought this was very inefficient. Why don't I just go into the HTML or CSS file and adjust the settings there? Because I still knew a bit about CSS files, I was more effective making these adjustments myself instead of having the LLM do everything and brute-force telling the LLM to move it this way and that way. I could just change them myself, refresh the page and see. It makes sense still to have an understanding of how these things work because there are cases where it is more efficient to do things yourself than prompt the LLM to redo everything. There's a middle ground where I do think there's still value in learning how things work.

items.question: Why do you see verifiable rewards as such an important part of training reasoning models?
items.object: Verifiable rewards in reasoning-model training
items.answer:
I think that's a really important point. Reasoning training is essentially mainly based on verifiable rewards, which means there are tasks where you can verify the answer. In DeepSeek R1 the verifiable rewards were coding and math. With math, for example, you ask the model to output the final answer in a boxed format in LaTeX. Then you can have deterministic regex or code to extract the answer, and then you can use something like Wolfram Alpha or SymPy to compare it to a reference answer. If 2 over 3 matches 2 over 3 or 4 over 6, it's essentially the same answer, but you can symbolically double-check the answer and get a reward signal whether it's correct or not.

This is great because you can evaluate infinite numbers of answers. With reinforcement learning with human feedback, you need human feedback essentially. You can train a reward model to approximate that, and it's part of the training where you get a score for each answer, but it's not quite as accurate as a really correct answer. With math, it's either correct or not. If you have something where you can verify the answer deterministically and cheaply, you can have the LLM generate infinite answers. You can say, "Generate 60,000 answers for this problem," and then calculate the reward on all of them in a very short time. It's still expensive to generate these answers, but you don't have vagueness and you don't have to have humans evaluating these answers. The same with code. In the DeepSeek R1 paper, the original approach was to have the code and make sure that the code compiles, basically. If it compiles correctly, you can use a code interpreter for that.

items.question: How do you see inference scaling contributing to stronger reasoning in LLMs?
items.object: Inference scaling for stronger LLM reasoning
items.answer:
I do think training is one part, but the other one is inference scaling. You can get much better performance if you use more compute. Inference scaling is essentially spending more compute after training, during inference, when someone uses the model to generate the answer. You can do it in multiple ways. Reasoning models themselves are already a form of inference scaling because they generate more tokens than regular models. The explanation is longer than a regular model provides, and it often helps the LLM to reach the correct answer. This is more like a sequential inference scaling.

You can also have parallel forms of inference scaling where you generate multiple answers. That's called self-consistency. If you have a math problem, you can have the LLM, with different temperature settings, answer the question multiple times, and then take a majority vote. There are different scoring methods or other LLMs that look at all the answers and give you the most likely correct answer. With that you can boost the performance of the model. It's more expensive, though. It's not a one-size-fits-all. You don't want to use it all the time. You use it when you need it.

items.question: How do you assess self-consistency and self-refinement as techniques for scaling LLM inference?
items.object: Self-consistency and self-refinement as inference-scaling techniques
items.answer:
I think of self-consistency and self-refinement as two examples of inference scaling. The biggest difference is one is a parallel technique, where self-consistency generates multiple answers, and you choose the correct answer based on majority vote, or you can have a scorer who assesses the answers. People call that technique best of n, best-of-n answer technique, like classic ensembling almost.

The other one is self-refinement, where you have the LLM generate the answer and then you feed the answer to another LLM or to itself and say, "Here's the answer. This is the question. Write a summary if the answer is likely answered correctly and what are weaknesses," like a rubric almost. You provide a rubric with certain things that the LLM should check, and then it gives you back a report and says, "This could be better. This is likely incorrect. The explanation doesn't match the final answer." Then you feed that output back to the original LLM and say, "Look at that report and refine your original answer based on the report here." Often this can lead to the LLM improving its own answer.

It's almost like this phenomenon: sometimes you ask ChatGPT something and it gives you something and you're like, "Wait, that can't be right." You tell it, "You are incorrect, you made a mistake," and it says, "Oh yeah, you are right, I made a mistake," and tries again and it's better next time. It's almost like that same mechanism where it self-refines its answers. Based on my experiments it can also sometimes make answers worse. It will overthink, or it was originally correct but then the feedback is weird or bad and it makes the answer incorrect. It's not a foolproof technique; it has caveats. In the DeepSeek Math 3.2 paper, where they had self-refinement in a more sophisticated way and a third model evaluating the evaluator, they showed how much the accuracy can improve. I don't know the numbers off the top of my head, but if they cranked up self-refinement and self-consistency, they were able to have gold-level performance in certain math competitions, which was very impressive given it was still the same model as they used before, but they just cranked up the inference scaling, basically.

items.question: How do you evaluate DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention and sparse attention as architectural advances?
items.object: DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention and sparse attention
items.answer:
DeepSeek version 3, besides the mixture of experts, had multi-head latent attention. It's a tweak of the attention mechanism where you have an intermediate smaller compressed state of the keys and values. The keys and values are important to compress because then your KV cache becomes smaller. You don't store the full keys and values in the KV cache, but a compressed form, and then you reconstruct the keys and values from the compressed form in inference. You're trading off compute with memory. You can think of it as LoRA, low-rank adaptation: you project it down into a compressed space and then project it up again. That's multi-head latent attention. That's an interesting tweak that people adopted in 2025 and 2026.

Then DeepSeek version 3.2 had another tweak, sparse attention. Sparse attention is not new, but there's always been research on how we make attention cheaper because it scales quadratically with sequence length, and there have been hundreds if not thousands of papers. With papers I'm always a bit careful. The ideas are interesting, but I'm waiting to see that in production, in quotation marks, to see it in a flagship model, because the idea might work well if you are only focused on a small model, but things may fall apart once you scale a model to 500 billion, 600 billion, one trillion parameters. DeepSeek is a nice case study because they have this flagship model, and if they use something in that flagship model, you know it works at scale. They have their own version of sparse attention, which I think they call DeepSparse Attention. Instead of one token paying attention to all the previous tokens, they have a lightning indexer, a small cheap model in a sense, that selects which tokens it pays attention to. It's kind of like a mask. You're calculating a mask over all the tokens to select a subset, to make it cheaper and scale sub-quadratically. These are tweaks, but it's not fundamentally changing how attention works. It's still the same attention mechanism, but how do we make it cheaper?

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for reliable continual learning that lets large language models improve themselves?
items.object: Reliable continual learning in large language models
items.answer:
I think this is maybe the biggest dream, in the sense of, "How can we make the model improve itself?" The biggest achievement right now that could be made if someone finds out a way this works. But right now there is no pathway to this. There's nothing really where you would say, "Oh, that's the thing that will give us reliable continual learning."

That being said, there are already forms of continual learning. It's more controlled: instead of the model automatically updating itself, people would collect data from the recent internet or recent tasks and then carefully update the model. It's not that we don't update models, but we also don't do it fully automatically. It's semi-automatic. It's not only because that's more reliable, because it's risky to just update a model on new data, but also because of resource constraints. I don't know how many copies of the model OpenAI has, but you definitely can't have a single copy per user. That would be way expensive. Everyone would have to have a little supercomputer at home or a $100,000 computer to have a big flagship model. Companies can't just update everything on the fly for each user because that would be infeasible.

Unless we have ways that the models only run on the personal device, I don't think we can have really good continual learning. The other thing is you have to be really careful how you update it. You don't want to make the model worse. It's such an important, expensive product. If you think about feeding the data back to OpenAI and then OpenAI automatically updates the model, maybe there's a bad update and it disrupts everything for everyone. I think it's more of an infrastructure security issue. Otherwise, if you look at the reasoning training, the reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, if you run this based on correct answers and that type of setting and just keep it running, it is kind of a form of continual learning in a sense. You can technically just keep running this; you just want to be more selective.

items.question: How do you see long-context LLMs changing the need for retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning on documents?

items.answer: Long-context LLMs have enabled so much recently. Before, people were building RAG systems, retrieval-augmented generation systems, and now it's almost, I wouldn't say they are obsolete. items.question: Where do you see the limits of using context and tools to keep an LLM informed instead of updating the model?
items.object: Context and tool use as substitutes for updating an LLM
items.answer: You could technically just provide all the relevant new information in context, but I think it only gets you so far because you as a user have to know what to provide as information. If you couple that with tool use, for example, if you ask about a historical event and the data cutoff is 2025 and you ask about a 2026 historical event, the LLM can still use a web search, still use a tool and look it up on the web. You don't necessarily need to update the LLM for that particular historical event. But if the historical event has a lot of ramifications and affects a lot of other things around it that might be missed, then you only get certain facts from a tool call but not that whole interaction with other data points. It's not fully replacing the updating, but it is making it maybe less necessary to do it, or not necessary to do it quite as often.

items.question: What interests you about text diffusion models as an alternative to transformer-based LLMs?

items.answer:

items.answer: I would say either way works. You don't have to read the first book. The second book uses a pre-trained LLM, so you don't have to pre-train your own LLM or need the first book to train the LLM for the second book. It's independent like that. But the second book doesn't explain in detail the pre-training or the architecture. I have an appendix on explaining the architecture, but it's not quite as detailed as the first book. If people want to understand the whole life cycle of an LLM from pre-training to post-training, it would make sense to read them sequentially, but you could also start with the second book, learn about inference scaling and reasoning, and then if you're interested in pre-training you can fill in the gaps later on. Either way works.
